title: The creed said together
hook: a whole congregation saying what they believe in one voice

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sermon, and the word homily. Your line was one line to keep. Which line from something you heard is still with you? Day one thousand three hundred forty-two.

The sermon ends. Nobody plays a note. The whole room stands, with a creak of benches and a shuffle of coats, and the minister begins: "I believe in one God." By the third word, everyone has caught up. Some people read from a card. Some have known it since they were small and don't look down at all. A teenager mutters it at half speed. An old man says every word like he's signing his name. Somewhere near the back, a woman pauses at a line she's wrestling with, then picks it up again at the next one. Then they sit down, and the service goes on. One long paragraph, said by a whole room in one voice. Today: the creed said together.

A creed is a short summary of the faith, said out loud. Christians trace the habit back to the New Testament. Start with Paul, writing to the church in Corinth. He hands on something he says was handed to him: "For I delivered unto you first of all that which I also received, how that Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures; And that he was buried, and that he rose again the third day according to the scriptures." Received, then delivered. A creed is passed from hand to hand, like a family recipe nobody wrote alone. Next, the mouth. In Romans, Paul puts belief and speech side by side: "For with the heart man believeth unto righteousness; and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation." In this picture, faith isn't only kept inside. It gets said. Then, the room. In some churches the Nicene Creed or the Apostles' Creed is said every Sunday. The old English prayer book has it begin, "I believe." Other churches say, "We believe." Either way, a whole congregation says it at once. Some Christians describe that as leaning on the church on a day when their own faith feels thin: nobody has to carry every word alone. Not every church recites a creed. Quakers and some Baptist churches, for example, prefer, for reasons of conscience, not to make any set words a test. Last, a father in Mark's Gospel. His son is suffering. Jesus tells him all things are possible to the one who believes, and the father cries out: "Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief." Both halves, in one breath. That line fits in a room full of people saying the creed together.
screen: `WITH THE MOUTH, NOT ONLY THE HEART.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say a creed aloud. Settle, and breathe. If you know one, say its opening line out loud, slowly, even if you're alone in the room. Notice what changes when the words leave your mouth instead of staying in your head. If you don't know one, read the line on the screen: I believe in one God the Father Almighty, Maker of heaven and earth. If you pray, you can add the father's words from Mark: Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief. If belief isn't where you are today, simply listen to the words as words other people say together, and notice which one stays with you. The bell holds the time.
screen: `I BELIEVE IN ONE GOD THE FATHER ALMIGHTY, MAKER OF HEAVEN AND EARTH.`

segments.voice: The creed said together. A short summary of the faith, handed on from one person to the next, and spoken aloud by a whole room at once.
Your line: we believe. Today, notice one thing you say together with other people, a pledge, a toast, a chorus, and listen to the room while you say it. Day one thousand three hundred forty-two.

howItsDone: In Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, Lutheran and some other churches, the congregation says or sings the Nicene Creed or the Apostles' Creed together during the service; Quakers and some Baptist churches do not recite a creed in worship.

Romans puts heart and mouth together: "with the mouth confession is made." in church it's said aloud, together.

options: "I believe, and I have no doubt at all."

fork.reveal: he says both at once: "Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief." belief and struggle in a single breath.

original.note: Greek: I believe, the verb Mark's father uses when he cries out to Jesus.

trapdoor: what you thought: a creed is a test of who's in and who's out.
what it means: a short summary of the faith, handed on and said aloud by a whole room together.
what a scholar hears: Paul's own words, delivered and received: he presents his summary as something passed to him, not something he made up.

notes: Review picks up day 1341 from the index (its script was not on disk when this was written).
'In some churches the Nicene Creed or the Apostles' Creed is said every Sunday' and 'Other churches say We believe': deliberately unquantified. Confirm.
Quakers and some Baptist churches described as not reciting creeds for reasons of conscience; confirm this is fair to both and that 'some' is right for Baptists.
BCP 1662 Nicene Creed opening quoted ('I believe in one God the Father Almighty, Maker of heaven and earth'); confirm exact wording and punctuation.
Mark 9:23 paraphrased ('all things are possible to the one who believes').
'Some Christians describe that as leaning on the church' is attributed, not asserted; confirm acceptable.
howItsDone lists churches that say the creed in worship; confirm the list.
Audit pass: narrator's 'the habit has roots in the New Testament itself' (a historical claim the creeds' later origins complicate) attributed: 'Christians trace the habit back to the New Testament.'

Editor pass: hook's 'a minute of speech' (a timing claim) cut; garbled Quaker/Baptist sentence rewritten; the son described as 'suffering' rather than 'ill' (Mark 9 describes a spirit); 'every church' myth reworded to vary the myth pattern across the week.
